extraction.name: Natural Questions
extraction.description: A question answering data set consisting of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. An annotator is presented with a question along with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results, and annotates a long answer (typically a paragraph) and a short answer (one or more entities) if present on the page, or marks null if no long/short answer is present.
extraction.creator: Google Research
extraction.citeAs: Tom Kwiatkowski et al. 2019. Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, vol. 7, pp. 453–466, 2019. https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl_a_00276
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. Questions are sampled from queries of 8 words or more that have been issued by multiple users in a short period of time. Simple heuristics are used to filter questions from the query stream. Questions are run through the Google search engine and those where there is a Wikipedia page in the top 5 search results are kept. The (question, Wikipedia page) pairs are the input to the human annotation task.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine, paired with Wikipedia pages from the top 5 search results.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions are filtered using heuristics: 1) start with 'who', 'when', or 'where' directly followed by: a) a finite form of 'do' or a modal verb; or b) a finite form of 'be' or 'have' with a verb in some later position; 2) start with 'who' directly followed by a verb that is not a finite form of 'be'; 3) contain multiple entities as well as an adjective, adverb, verb, or determiner; 4) contain a categorical noun phrase immediately preceded by a preposition or relative clause; 5) end with a categorical noun phrase, and do not contain a preposition or relative clause. Questions are run through the Google search engine and kept only if there is a Wikipedia page in the top 5 search results.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: An annotator is presented with a (question, Wikipedia page) pair. The annotation task is divided into three conceptual stages: 1) Question Identification: Contributors determine whether the given question is good or bad. A good question is a fact-seeking question that can be answered with an entity or explanation. A bad question is ambiguous, incomprehensible, dependent on clear false presuppositions, opinion-seeking, or not clearly a request for factual information. 2) Long Answer Identification: For good questions only, annotators select the earliest HTML bounding box containing enough information for a reader to completely infer the answer to the question. Bounding boxes can be paragraphs, tables, list items, or whole lists. Alternatively, annotators mark 'no answer' if the page does not answer the question, or if the information is present but not contained in a single one of the allowed elements. 3) Short Answer Identification: For examples with long answers, annotators select the entity or set of entities within the long answer that answer the question. Alternatively, annotators can flag that the short answer is yes, no, or they can flag that no short answer is possible.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Post hoc evaluation of annotation quality was performed using consensus judgments from four experts. Experts categorized (question, long answer) pairs into three categories: Correct (C) - clear beyond a reasonable doubt that the answer is correct; Correct (but debatable) (Cd) - a reasonable person could be satisfied by the answer; however, a reasonable person could raise a reasonable doubt about the answer; Wrong (W) - there is not convincing evidence that the answer is correct. 25-way annotations on 302 examples were collected to study human variability on the annotation task. The correlation between the proportion of annotators marking non-null answers and annotation precision was analyzed.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Single annotations for 307,373 training examples; 5-way annotations for 7,830 development examples and 7,842 test examples; 25-way annotations on 302 examples for variability analysis
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Questions are focused on longer queries (8 words or more) as they are more complex and thus a more challenging test for deep NLU. Questions beginning with 'how to' are excluded by the filters. The data focuses on Wikipedia as a source of factual information, which may introduce biases inherent to Wikipedia's content and style.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The data focuses on longer queries (8 words or more in length) and excludes 'how to' questions. The data is limited to Wikipedia as the evidence source, which may not be representative of other sources of factual information on the Web. For naturally occurring questions there is often genuine ambiguity in whether or not an answer is acceptable, and there are often a number of acceptable answers. Annotators can disagree about whether a document contains an answer to a question, and about the location of the best answer when multiple valid answers exist in distinct locations.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation. The dataset is designed as a benchmark for question answering research, specifically for open-domain question answering that requires natural language understanding. The task is designed to be close to an end-to-end question answering application. The input to a model is a question together with an entire Wikipedia page. The target output from the model is: 1) a long-answer (e.g., a paragraph) from the page that answers the question, or alternatively an indication that there is no answer on the page; 2) a short answer where applicable.
